title: Assessing the efficacy of polyacrylamide hydrogel which is injected into the joints of patients suffering from arthritis in their synovial joints (knee, shoulder etc) instead of steroid injections or joint replacement surgery
official: Intra-articular Polyacrylamide hydrogel for Synovial Joint Arthritis. A comprehensive review of the efficacy of Polyacrylamide hydrogel in patients for whom a steroid injection or arthroplasty is warranted
summary:
Background and study aims  
Osteoarthritis is a common condition that causes pain, stiffness, and reduced movement in joints such as the knee, shoulder, hip, or ankle. Many people are treated with pain relief medicines or steroid injections, and some may eventually need joint replacement surgery. This study is looking at whether a gel injection called polyacrylamide hydrogel can reduce pain and improve joint movement for people with osteoarthritis. The aim is to see if this injection could be a longer lasting and less invasive option than repeated steroid injections or surgery.

Who can participate?  
Adults aged 18 years or over who have ongoing pain from osteoarthritis or other similar joint problems may be able to take part. Participants need to have symptoms that have not improved enough with standard treatments and where their clinician believes a joint injection is appropriate. People with joint infections, certain inflammatory joint diseases, recent surgery or injections to the same joint, or who are pregnant or breastfeeding will not be able to take part.

What does the study involve?
Participants will receive a single injection of polyacrylamide hydrogel into the affected joint as part of their usual NHS care. The injection will be guided by ultrasound, given under local anaesthetic, and carried out by trained clinicians using sterile techniques. After the injection, participants will be followed for up to two years. During this time, they will be asked to complete questionnaires about their pain, joint function, and quality of life. Most follow-up will be done remotely, so extra hospital visits are usually not needed. Information about any side effects, further treatments, or later surgery will also be collected.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?  
Some participants may experience reduced pain, better movement, and an improved quality of life, although these benefits cannot be guaranteed. The risks are similar to those of standard joint injections and may include short term pain, swelling, or bruising at the injection site. Infection is rare. It is also possible that the injection may not improve symptoms.

Where is the study run from?  
The study is run from University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust, with plans to include other hospitals across the United Kingdom.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?  
The study is expected to start after ethics approval, with the first participants planned from December 2027. It is expected to run until January 2029.

Who is funding the study?  
University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust (UK).

Who is the main contact?  
Dr Togay Koc, togay.koc@uhs.nhs.uk
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Adults aged 18 years or over
2. Diagnosis of symptomatic synovial joint pathology considered suitable for intra-articular injection by the treating clinician.
3. Clinical and/or radiological evidence of joint disease affecting the target joint
4. Persistent symptoms despite standard conservative management, including pharmacological and/or non-pharmacological treatment where appropriate
5. Ability to understand the study requirements and provide written informed consent
6. Willingness and ability to comply with study procedures and follow-up assessments
Exclusion criteria:
1. Age under 18 years
2. Active local infection at the injection site or systemic infection
3. Previous intra-articular injection to the target joint within the preceding 6 months
4. Previous surgery to the target joint within the preceding 6 months or planned surgery during the study period
5. Known hypersensitivity or contraindication to the study intervention, local anaesthetic, or antibiotic prophylaxis
6. Known coagulopathy or current anticoagulant therapy where injection is contraindicated
7. Diagnosis of inflammatory arthropathy (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis) or other systemic inflammatory joint disease affecting the target joint
8. Pregnancy or breastfeeding
9. Inability to complete study procedures or follow-up assessments
10. Any medical, psychological, or social condition which, in the opinion of the investigator, would make participation unsuitable or place the participant at undue risk
11. Only participants with capacity to provide informed consent will be included
12. Individuals lacking capacity to consent will not be recruited
